1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: A 56-year-old female patient presented with "dry cough for 2 months, fever, blood-streaked sputum, and hearing loss for 2 weeks." In approximately 2 months before Day 0, she developed a dry cough without an obvious precipitating factor, occurring mostly during the daytime and characterized as a continuous irritative cough. She had no chest pain, chest tightness, fever, or other discomfort. She sought care at a local hospital, where chest CT showed scattered flocculent opacities in both lungs. She was treated with "moxifloxacin" for infection for 1 week, and her symptoms improved somewhat, but there was no significant change on imaging. On Day 0, repeat chest CT showed the lesions remained similar to before. On Day +1, she developed chills and fever, Tmax 38.9℃; the cough worsened again, with intermittent blood-streaked sputum, accompanied by rapidly progressive bilateral hearing loss. She subsequently received anti-infective treatment with "cefmetazole + levofloxacin," "piperacillin-tazobactam + moxifloxacin," and "Tienam + vancomycin + voriconazole." After treatment, none of the above symptoms improved, and her temperature instead gradually increased. On Day +15, repeat chest CT continued to show marked progression of multiple bilateral pulmonary lesions compared with before. Past medical history: denied chronic diseases such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia; denied infectious disease history such as hepatitis and TB. In 2017, she underwent surgery for "right mammary lobular hyperplasia." In 2017, she was diagnosed with "bilateral chronic sinusitis, bilateral secretory otitis media, and right nasal polyp" and subsequently underwent sinusotomy, right nasal polypectomy, and tympanostomy tube placement, but postoperative nasal obstruction and hearing loss did not improve. She had a 6-month history of diabetes insipidus, treated with oral desmopressin, with relatively good control. She denied any history of blood transfusion and denied food or drug allergies. She had no history of smoking, alcohol use, or special dust exposure. Marital/reproductive history and family history were unremarkable. Physical examination: T 36.8℃, P 80/min, R 20/min, BP 120/70mmHg. She was alert. There was no rash on the skin. No abnormal nasal secretions were present, and there was no tenderness over the paranasal sinus areas. No abnormal secretion was present in the external auditory canals. Bilateral hearing was significantly decreased. No cyanosis of the lips. Dentition was regular. Breath sounds were coarse in both lungs, with no dry or wet rales heard. No abnormalities were found on examination of the heart, abdomen, spine, extremities, or nervous system. Laboratory tests: Blood tests (Day -52): HbA1c and fasting blood glucose were normal. Adenohypophyseal hormone-related tests were normal. ANA and anticentromere antibody were both negative. Albumin 35g/L, sodium 149mmol/L, chloride 113.1mmol/L; the remaining liver and kidney function indices were normal. PCT and G test were normal. Two sputum cultures (Day -49): Candida albicans. Acid-fast stain (Day -46): negative. Non-contrast chest CT (Day -52): scattered infectious lesions in both lungs, with mild focal bronchial dilatation. Non-contrast chest CT (Day -44): scattered infectious lesions in both lungs, with mild focal bronchial dilatation; compared with the film from Day -52, some lesions in both lungs were slightly absorbed. Non-contrast chest CT (Day 0): bilateral pulmonary infection with bronchitic changes. Temporal bone/mastoid CT (Day +11): bilateral chronic otomastoiditis; right tympanic membrane perforation considered. Sinusitis, postoperative changes? Non-contrast chest CT (Day +17): compared with the prior film (Day 0), bronchitis with multiple infections in both lungs, with obvious progression. Blood tests (Day +11): white blood cells 9.3*10^9/L, N% 73.0%, L% 15.7%, Hb 124g/L, platelets 361*10^9/L, CRP 107.64mg/L. Autoimmune antibodies (ANA, full ENA panel, anti-dsDNA, anti-GBM, PR3-, MPO-ANCA), tumor markers, influenza virus nucleic acid, EBV-IgM, CMV-IgM, total IgE, and G test were all unremarkable. Sputum smear (Day -49): fungal spores found. Two acid-fast stains were negative. Urinalysis (Day -46): urine specific gravity 1.010, red blood cells 11.0/ul, occult blood +-.

differential_diagnoses.name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, ANCA-associated vasculitis)
supporting_evidence: There is evidence of simultaneous involvement of the upper and lower respiratory tracts: in 2017, the patient was diagnosed with "bilateral chronic sinusitis, bilateral secretory otitis media, and right nasal polyp"; after surgery, nasal obstruction and hearing loss did not improve; this time, "abrupt bilateral hearing loss" occurred again.

Pulmonary involvement presented as "dry cough for 2 months, fever, hemoptysis accompanied by hearing loss for 2 weeks," and chest CT showed scattered/multiple lesions in both lungs, with "marked progression" on Day +17 compared with Day 0.

Poor response to anti-infective therapy: after sequential use of multiple broad-spectrum antibacterial and antifungal regimens, "the above symptoms showed no improvement, and body temperature instead gradually increased"
Clues suggestive of small-vessel vasculitis/renal involvement: urinalysis showed "RBC 11.0/ul, occult blood +-"
Imaging shows gradually progressive multiple patchy lesions in both lungs, consistent with possible inflammatory/vasculitic pulmonary parenchymal lesions
The combination of hemoptysis, fever, ENT involvement, and multiple pulmonary lesions is highly suggestive of GPA.
opposing_evidence: PR3- and MPO-ANCA both showed no abnormalities
Renal function indices were normal, with no clear evidence of progressive renal impairment
Physical examination showed no abnormal nasal secretions in the nasal cavity, no tenderness over the paranasal sinus region, and no positive findings on active nasal examination.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious pneumonia (drug-resistant bacterial or atypical pathogen)
supporting_evidence: Fever, Tmax 38.9℃, accompanied by worsening cough and blood-streaked sputum
CRP 107.64mg/L is elevated, suggesting a marked inflammatory response
Multiple chest CT reports described "scattered infectious lesions in both lungs," "bilateral pulmonary infection with bronchitic changes," and "bilateral bronchitis with multiple infections."
Imaging shows multiple patchy lesions in both lungs, with marked progression on Day +17 compared with Day 0, as can be seen in progression of infectious pneumonia
opposing_evidence: The disease course has reached 2 months; in the early stage it was predominantly an irritating dry cough, which is not consistent with the typical onset characteristics of acute bacterial pneumonia.
After sequential treatment with "moxifloxacin," "cefmetazole + levofloxacin," "piperacillin-tazobactam + moxifloxacin," and "Tienam + vancomycin + voriconazole," there was no improvement.
PCT was unremarkable, not supporting typical invasive bacterial infection
WBC 9.3*10^9/L, with only a neutrophil percentage of 73.0%, without very prominent blood count findings suggestive of bacterial infection

differential_diagnoses.name: Invasive fungal infection (such as pulmonary aspergillosis)
supporting_evidence: Sputum smear: "fungal spores identified"; 2 sputum cultures: "Candida albicans"
Fever and blood-streaked sputum, with progressive progression of multiple pulmonary lesions, may be seen in fungal pulmonary infection.
No response to broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy, suggesting that nonbacterial pathogens should be considered
Imaging showed multiple lesions in both lungs, with marked progression over a short period.
opposing_evidence: G test showed no abnormalities
No definite history of immunosuppression; denies a history of chronic diseases such as diabetes, and fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin are normal
Sputum culture positive for Candida albicans more often suggests colonization and cannot directly confirm invasive pulmonary fungal infection.
No improvement after combined treatment with voriconazole

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease
supporting_evidence: Prolonged course; dry cough for 2 months, followed by fever and blood-streaked sputum
Chest CT showed scattered/multiple lesions in both lungs, with mild dilation of some bronchi; mycobacterial infection may have similar manifestations
Poor response to empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
opposing_evidence: Denies a history of TB or other infectious diseases
Two acid-fast stains were negative
No more typical imaging clues of mycobacterial infection, such as cavitation or tree-in-bud pattern, were seen on imaging description.
Stage 1 information did not provide a clear history of TB exposure or an immunosuppressive background

differential_diagnoses.name: Anti-GBM disease or other pulmonary-renal syndrome
supporting_evidence: The presence of "blood-streaked sputum" suggests the possibility of alveolar hemorrhage.
Urinalysis showed “red blood cells 11.0/ul, occult blood +-”, suggesting possible concomitant glomerular involvement.
Rapid progression of multiple bilateral lung lesions, seen in diseases associated with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
opposing_evidence: Anti-GBM antibody: no abnormality
Liver and kidney function indices showed no abnormalities, and there was no evidence of renal injury such as elevated serum creatinine.
There is definite ENT involvement, including chronic sinusitis, otitis media, and hearing loss, favoring GPA rather than isolated anti-GBM disease.
The imaging report favors an infectious lesion; typical diffuse ground-glass opacities were not described in the first stage.

differential_diagnoses.name: Organizing pneumonia (cryptogenic or secondary)
supporting_evidence: At disease onset, the main manifestation was a persistent irritating dry cough, with a lack of typical early infectious toxemia symptoms.
Chest CT shows multiple patchy lesions in both lungs, persistent over time and progressive, which can be seen in organizing pneumonia
Poor response to multiple anti-infective treatments suggests possible atypical infectious inflammation or immune-related lung disease
opposing_evidence: In the later stage, high fever, markedly elevated CRP, and blood-streaked sputum developed, which are not common in typical organizing pneumonia.
Accompanied by chronic sinusitis, otitis media, and markedly decreased hearing, suggesting an underlying systemic disease; simple organizing pneumonia cannot adequately explain the ENT manifestations
The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

recommended_exams.exam: Infection-related markers (endotoxin, G test, cryptococcal latex agglutination test, T-SPOT)
BALF (acid-fast staining, bacterial culture, fungi, GM test)

stage2_input.text: Further evaluation after admission: Arterial blood gas analysis (on room air): pH 7.47, pCO2 36.9 mmHg, pO2 81 mmHg, HCO3- 26.6 mmol/L, SO2 96.7%. Infection-related markers: endotoxin, G test, cryptococcal latex agglutination test, T-SPOT: negative. Sputum acid-fast stain (-), sputum culture: Candida albicans. Liver and kidney function: hypoalbuminemia, with no other obvious abnormalities. Coagulation function: D-dimer 1220 ug/L, PT and APTT mildly prolonged. Tumor markers and lymphocyte subsets: no obvious abnormalities. Urinalysis: urine specific gravity <1.005, occult blood 3+, red blood cells 107.1/ul, non-uniform morphology. Electronic bronchoscopy: mild hyperemia of the bilateral bronchial mucosa, with no positive findings on pathogen testing. BALF: acid-fast testing, bacterial culture, fungal testing, and GM test were all negative. BALF-mNGS: no specific pathogen detected. On Day +21, polydipsia and polyuria worsened significantly, with 24-hour urine output reaching 5600 ml. Repeat urinalysis: urine occult blood 1+, with no other abnormalities; serum Na+ 146 umol/L, serum Cl- 112 umol/L. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI showed absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot on the T1WI sequence, consistent with central diabetes insipidus. Repeat chest CT showed marked progression of multiple bilateral lung lesions compared with before, with partial consolidation in the superior segment of the right lower lobe and the basal segments of the right lower lobe. Repeat p-ANCA and MPO-ANCA were positive.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immediately perform CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had a dry cough for 2 months and developed fever and hemoptysis over the past 2 weeks. Chest CT showed persistent marked progression of multiple bilateral pulmonary lesions, and sequential treatment with multiple broad-spectrum antibacterial and antifungal therapies was ineffective. At the same time, there was concomitant sinus/middle ear involvement, rapidly progressive hearing loss, urinary abnormalities, central diabetes insipidus, and subsequent positivity for p-ANCA and MPO-ANCA, suggesting that, in addition to infection, vasculitis-related pulmonary involvement should also be strongly suspected. Previous sputum culture, acid-fast staining, BALF culture, GM test, and mNGS did not identify a definite pathogen, yet the imaging continued to worsen; therefore, direct acquisition of tissue from the pulmonary parenchymal lesions is needed. CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy can obtain samples from the progressive pulmonary lesions under imaging guidance, with the main goal of determining whether the lesions represent infection, tumor, organizing inflammation, or vasculitis-related inflammatory injury, thereby providing key evidence for whether to initiate glucocorticoid/immunosuppressive therapy subsequently and, as much as possible, avoiding the risk of blindly intensifying immunosuppression when the pathogen remains unclear.

This case had a complex clinical presentation, with fever, hemoptysis in sputum, and multiple progressive pulmonary lesions, as well as upper respiratory tract and ear involvement, occult blood in urine, and central diabetes insipidus; both infection and ANCA-associated vasculitis needed to be differentiated. Extensive prior infectious workup was negative and anti-infective treatment failed; imaging and serology alone were still insufficient to exclude infection, tumor, or other inflammatory lung diseases. Pathologic examination was the key confirmatory step after the lung puncture specimen was obtained, allowing direct observation of whether inflammation, hemorrhage, necrosis, granuloma formation, blood vessel wall involvement, or tumor cells were present in the alveolar spaces, alveolar septa, and interstitium, thereby clarifying the nature of the lesion at the histologic level. Its clinical significance lies in providing tissue evidence for the diagnosis of systemic vasculitis, or at least supportive inflammatory evidence, while excluding infectious or neoplastic diseases that require completely different treatment pathways, thereby guiding whether to use glucocorticoids and subsequent immunosuppressive regimens.

The patient's pulmonary lesions were persistent and rapidly progressive, accompanied by fever and blood-tinged sputum. Fungal spores had previously been seen on sputum smear, and sputum culture had previously grown Candida albicans. Although the G test, BALF fungal studies, and the response to voriconazole treatment did not support invasive fungal infection, further histopathologic evaluation is still needed to distinguish fungal colonization from true infection. PAS staining was performed on the lung biopsy specimen primarily to look for histopathologic evidence of pathogens rich in polysaccharide components, such as fungi, in order to answer the key clinical question of whether the lesion was caused by fungal infection. A negative PAS result helps reduce the likelihood that fungal infection is the main cause of pulmonary progression, strengthens the assessment of noninfectious inflammatory/vasculitic pulmonary involvement, reduces the risk of mistakenly treating an infectious lesion as vasculitis with immunosuppressive therapy, and supports subsequent treatment direction toward vasculitis control.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Immediately perform CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy. One week later, pathology reported: the biopsy specimen from the "right middle lobe" showed intra-alveolar congestion, widened alveolar septa, interstitial fibrous tissue proliferation, and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration, suggesting inflammatory changes (PAS stain negative; no evidence of fungal infection identified).

diagnostic_basis: Middle-aged woman, insidious onset, long disease course, acute progression

Nasal obstruction and hearing loss were the initial symptoms, followed by diabetes insipidus, fever, blood-streaked sputum, and microscopic hematuria; prior surgical treatment and anti-infective therapy were ineffective, while glucocorticoid therapy was effective.
ESR and CRP ↑, urine occult blood 3+, p-ANCA and MPO-ANCA positive
Imaging showed multiple infiltrative opacities in both lungs and loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot.
Lung biopsy pathology suggested inflammatory changes
According to the 2017 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for GPA, the diagnosis of GPA is established

treatment_plan: Methylprednisolone 80 mg anti-inflammatory treatment for 2 weeks
After discharge, prednisone 50 mg was given orally once daily; thereafter the corticosteroid dose was gradually tapered.

In approximately 11 months after Day 0, when the glucocorticoid dose was tapered to 5 mg, recurrent pulmonary lesions occurred. The local hospital increased the glucocorticoid dose and added tacrolimus; after stabilization, the dose was gradually tapered.
treatment_response: After treatment with methylprednisolone, the patient's body temperature quickly returned to normal, hemoptysis resolved, and symptoms of nasal congestion, hearing impairment, polydipsia, and polyuria also improved significantly.

At 1-month post-discharge follow-up, chest CT showed that the multiple lesions in both lungs had basically been absorbed; urine occult blood turned negative; desmopressin was discontinued; pituitary function recovered.
At 3-month follow-up, no new lesions were found in either lung, and ANCA turned negative.
In approximately 11 months after Day 0, recurrent pulmonary lesions occurred when the glucocorticoid dose was tapered to 5 mg; after increasing the dose, the condition is currently stable.
